title: Risks of Working With Recruiting Agencies: Cost and Incentives (November 2026)
summary: How agency fees, guarantee periods, and speed-first incentives can work against startups hiring early, and how a recruiter marketplace changes the math.
body_markdown:
Your first engineer or first head of sales starts on a Monday, and the agency invoice for 20% to 25% of their salary lands the same week. If that person is a poor fit, you may not know for several months, and by then the agency’s guarantee window may have already closed. For a startup where each early hire shapes the product, the culture, and the runway, understanding the[risks of working with recruiting agencies](https://www.dover.com/) before you sign is part of the hiring decision itself.


**TLDR:**


-


Agency fees commonly run 15% to 25% of first-year salary, so a single early hire can cost $25,000 or more before any internal time is counted.


-


Most agencies earn their fee on placement, which can reward speed and an accepted offer more than a long-term fit.


-


Guarantee periods often run 30 to 90 days, so the incentive can be to present a candidate who gets through the window, not one who thrives for years.


-


Early startup roles are often the hardest to fill and the easiest to deprioritize, because the search is slow, the scope is fuzzy, and the payoff is uncertain.


-


Some marketplace models let you choose how a recruiter is paid (hourly, retained, or per hire) and have them work inside your own hiring pipeline, which changes both the cost and the incentives.


## Why the Agency Model Creates Risk for Early Hires


A recruiting agency is a business with its own revenue targets, and most of its structure is built around closing placements. That is not a flaw in any individual recruiter, but it does shape what a recruiter is rewarded for, and a founder buying a search should know which behaviors the fee structure encourages.


For a growth-stage company filling a standard role, those incentives often line up reasonably well with what the hiring manager wants. For a seed or Series A startup hiring its first few people, they can drift apart. Early roles tend to have shifting scopes, thin job descriptions, equity-heavy compensation, and candidates who need to be persuaded rather than simply matched. Those are searches where fit matters more than speed, and where a mismatch is costly, as the broader[contingency recruiting incentive problem](https://www.dover.com/blog/contingency-recruiting-placement-fee-incentives) explains.


## Agency Risks at a Glance


Risk What it looks like with an agency What changes with hourly or retained marketplace pricing


Cost scales with salary Fee is a percentage of first-year pay, so senior and technical hires cost the most Cost follows hours worked and is not tied to the candidate’s pay


Speed incentive Revenue arrives when an offer is accepted, so closing fast is rewarded Recruiter is paid for the work, so slowing down to calibrate does not cost them the fee


Guarantee-window horizon Success may be measured by whether the hire stays 30 to 90 days Success is judged by you inside a shared pipeline, with no payout hinging on a day count


Salary pressure A higher accepted salary raises the fee No fee link to the offer amount


Hard-to-fill roles Slow searches compete with easier placements for recruiter attention Hours are directed where you point them


Process visibility Sourcing and outreach often sit in the agency’s systems Recruiter works in your ATS, so history stays with you


Candidate pool after the hire You typically receive the placed candidate, while the rest of the sourced pool stays with the agency Every sourced and screened candidate stays in your pipeline to revisit if a hire does not work out


Commitment Exclusivity or retainer terms may limit your options No long-term contract


## The Cost Risk: Fees That Scale With Salary


Most contingency agencies charge a percentage of the candidate’s first-year compensation, with 15% to 25% a common range, as the[breakdown of tech recruiter fees](https://www.dover.com/blog/tech-recruiter-fees-cost-guide) lays out. On a $150,000 engineering hire, that is $22,500 to $37,500. For context, SHRM’s benchmarking data puts the[average non-executive cost per hire at $5,475](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/news/talent-acquisition/real-costs-recruitment) , which means an agency placement on a senior role can cost several times a typical hire.


The structure also has a quieter effect on cost. Because the fee tracks salary, the agency benefits when the accepted offer is higher. Recruiters are not necessarily acting in bad faith when they advocate for a candidate’s compensation, but a startup with a tight budget and a mostly equity-based offer is the party absorbing that pressure.


Three details inside the contract can raise the real price further:


-


**The fee basis.** Some agreements calculate the fee on total compensation, including signing bonuses and guaranteed variable pay, not base salary alone.


-


**Expenses and minimums.** Advertising, assessments, and minimum fees may be billed separately.


-


**Tail periods.** Candidates the agency introduced can trigger a fee if you hire them months later, even for a different role.


A[recruitment fee agreement](https://www.dover.com/blog/recruitment-fee-agreements-negotiate-clauses) is negotiable, and these clauses are worth reading line by line.


## The Incentive Risk: Paid to Close, Not to Retain


An agency running on contingency earns nothing until an offer is accepted and a start date arrives. That creates a natural pressure to get a candidate over the line, and to spend effort on the searches most likely to close.


For a startup, two behaviors are worth watching for:


-


**Candidate steering.** A recruiter juggling several searches may present the candidates who are most likely to accept quickly, not the ones who best match your unusual stage, stack, or working style.


-


**Deprioritized searches.** A founding-engineer or first-GTM search can take many weeks of sourcing with an uncertain payoff, while a standard mid-level role closes faster for a comparable fee. Recruiter time tends to flow to the easier placement.


None of this requires bad intent. It follows from how the revenue is earned, which is why the structure matters more than the individual recruiter.


## The Guarantee-Period Risk


Most agencies offer some form of guarantee: if the hire leaves within a set window, the agency runs a replacement search or issues a partial credit. These windows commonly fall between 30 and 90 days, and the exact terms vary by contract.


A guarantee sounds like protection, and it has real value. It also defines the period during which the agency has a financial stake in the hire staying. After the window closes, the fee is typically earned in full.


That produces a mismatch between what the agency is covered for and what your startup actually needs:


-


An early hire’s real performance often does not show until the second or third quarter, once the onboarding is finished and the ambiguity of a startup role starts to test them.


-


A person who is polite, capable at interviews, and unlikely to quit in their first 90 days can satisfy the guarantee without being the right long-term hire.


-


A hire who leaves at day 91, or who stays but underperforms, falls outside the guarantee entirely.


Even inside the window, a guarantee is rarely a cash refund. Many agreements offer a replacement search or a credit, and they may exclude departures tied to role changes or layoffs. Your team still absorbs the repeat interviews, the lost ramp-up time, and the empty seat. The[guarantee terms in your agreement](https://www.dover.com/blog/recruitment-fee-agreements-negotiate-clauses) are where this risk is either contained or left open.


## Why Early Hires Make Every Risk Larger


The same agency risks apply at any company, but they compound for early-stage teams for a few reasons.


**Early roles are hard to define.** A first product hire or first sales lead often requires judgment about scope that the hiring manager is still working out. An agency that is paid to fill a defined spec may fill the spec and miss the need.


**Your pitch is harder.** Candidates weighing a seed-stage company against a stable employer need to be convinced on equity, mission, and founder trust. A recruiter with limited context on your company may not tell that story well, and a founder who is not in the conversation cannot correct it.


**Mistakes cost more.** With a team of eight, one wrong hire changes the culture, slows the roadmap, and consumes the founders’ time, a pattern described in guidance on[recruiter red flags for startups](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-recruiter-red-flags-12-signs) .


**Runway is finite.** A large placement fee on one early hire is a meaningful fraction of a month’s burn, and an additional replacement fee after a miss compounds it.


## The Visibility Risk: A Search You Cannot See


When an agency runs a search, sourcing activity, outreach messages, and candidate notes typically live inside the agency’s own systems. You see a shortlist, not the funnel behind it.


That limits your ability to correct course. If the outreach pitch undersells the company, or the agency is sourcing from the wrong pool, you may only learn about it weeks later when the slate looks off. When the engagement ends, the pipeline history often stays with the agency, so the next search starts from scratch. If the hire does not work out, the runners-up and the rest of the screened slate are not yours to go back to.


## What Changes in a Recruiter Marketplace Model


A recruiter marketplace connects a company with independent recruiters instead of a single agency. Because each recruiter sets their own pricing, a marketplace can offer several models side by side: hourly, retained, and contingency (pay per hire). The incentives differ by model, and the marketplace structure around them changes how much those incentives can hurt you. The[agency versus marketplace comparison](https://www.dover.com/blog/startup-agency-recruiting-vs-recruiter-marketplace) covers the choice in more depth.


Where the hourly model helps most:


-


**Cost follows effort, not salary.** A recruiter’s pay is not tied to what the candidate is paid, so there is no financial reason to push a higher offer.


-


**No race to the window.** With no fee that depends on a day count, a recruiter has less reason to optimize for a short retention window and more room to spend time on calibration.


-


**Shared visibility.** When the recruiter works inside your own hiring pipeline, you see sourcing, outreach, and stage movement as it happens.


Each model carries its own risk. A recruiter paid for hours has no direct financial stake in the outcome, and a poorly managed engagement can run long. A retained recruiter is paid for committed capacity, so you are relying on their effort and your ability to check it. A contingency recruiter on a marketplace still has a reason to close quickly. What offsets these risks is the structure around the fee: visibility into the work, short commitments, a pipeline you keep, and clear expectations, which is why[how you vet and manage external recruiters](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-vet-external-recruiters-for-your-startup) matters in any model.


## How Dover’s Recruiter Marketplace Is Structured


Dover pairs a free ATS with a marketplace of fractional recruiters who have startup hiring backgrounds. Each recruiter sets their own pricing, so you can choose the model that fits the search: hourly, retained, or contingency (pay per hire). That lets you match the incentive to the role, for example hourly or retained for a hard, ambiguous first hire where fit matters more than speed, and per-hire pricing for a well-defined role. Across Dover’s marketplace, hires average about $4,800 each, though the figure varies with role seniority and the hours a search requires, and the[cost-per-hire data](https://www.dover.com/recruiters#cost-per-hire) is published by role.


A few structural points answer the risks above:


-


**Shared pipeline.** Recruiters can work inside your Dover ATS alongside your team, so sourcing notes, outreach history, and candidate stages remain in your account when the engagement ends.


-


**You keep the whole pipeline, not just the hire.** Every candidate a recruiter sources and screens in your account stays there, including the finalists who did not get the offer. If a hire does not work out, you can go back to a pool of already-qualified people instead of paying for a new search from zero.


-


**Low-risk start.** Companies begin with an $800 refundable deposit, and there is no long-term contract, so you can change course if a recruiter is not the right match. The[refundable deposit model](https://www.dover.com/blog/refundable-recruiter-deposits) is explained separately.


-


**Less pressure to game a guarantee window.** With hourly or retained pricing, the recruiter is not paid a fee that depends on a retention date, so the engagement is not organized around getting a hire through the first 30 to 90 days. If you choose a contingency recruiter, ask what guarantee applies, since that term is set by the recruiter.


The model does not remove the need for judgment. You still decide who to hire, and a marketplace works best when a founder or hiring manager stays involved in the search. Agencies remain a reasonable choice for a single, urgent, well-scoped search, or for roles where you need a network you do not have.


## Questions to Ask Before You Sign With Any Agency


-


How is the fee calculated: base salary only, or total compensation?


-


How long is the guarantee, when does the clock start, and is the remedy a replacement, a credit, or a refund?


-


Which departures are excluded from the guarantee?


-


What exclusivity, retainer, or tail-period terms apply?


-


What share of the agency’s recent placements in similar roles were still in seat after a year?


-


Will I see sourcing and outreach activity, or only a final shortlist?


-


Who owns the candidate data after the search ends?


## FAQs


### What happens if an agency hire leaves after the guarantee period ends?


Once the guarantee window closes, the placement fee is typically fully earned and the agency owes you nothing further. Any replacement is a new search, and depending on the contract it may carry a second placement fee. That is why the length of the window, the start date it runs from, and what counts as a covered departure are worth reading closely before you sign.


### Do agency guarantees refund the placement fee?


Often they do not. Many agreements offer a replacement search or a partial credit instead of a cash refund, and the terms may exclude departures tied to role changes, layoffs, or restructuring. Your team’s repeat interviewing and onboarding time is rarely covered either way.


### Are recruiting agencies a bad choice for startups?


No. Agencies can be a good fit for a single, well-defined, urgent search, or when you need access to a candidate network you do not have. The risks in this article are structural, not a verdict on any one firm, and they matter most when the role is an early hire with unclear scope and a long ramp-up.


### How can a startup test an agency before committing?


Ask for sample candidate slates from recent searches in similar roles, the share of placements that stayed past a year, and the full contract before any verbal commitment. Prefer short exclusivity windows, base-salary-only fee calculation, and written terms for what counts as a covered departure.


## Final Thoughts on Recruiting Agency Risk for Startups


The risk in working with an agency is less about any single recruiter and more about what the fee structure rewards: a closed placement, a salary-linked price, and a retention window that ends long before an early hire’s real impact is clear. For a startup, the useful question is which of those exposures your specific search can afford. A defined, urgent role with a short ramp may tolerate them, while a first engineering or sales hire often does not. If you are comparing options, Dover is one place to look: a free ATS paired with fractional recruiters who work inside your own pipeline and choose between hourly, retained, and contingency pricing, averaging about $4,800 per hire with no long-term contract.
